title: Error Bars and Storm Cones
objective: After this level you can read error bars and a hurricane forecast cone as ranges of uncertainty, not as sizes.
summary: Error bars and hurricane cones draw uncertainty, not size. NHC's cone holds two-thirds of past track errors, so the storm's center strays outside about one time in three.

cards.headline: A hurricane cone looks like a picture of the storm. It isn't.
cards.body: Neither are the little whiskers on a bar chart. Both draw uncertainty: a range where the truth probably lies. Read them as sizes and you'll get the wrong idea.

cards.headline: Whiskers mean "somewhere in here"
cards.body: An estimate is rarely one exact number. The Royal Statistical Society suggests saying "between 190 and 210" rather than just "200", and drawing that range as error bars or shaded areas. The bar shows the estimate; the whiskers show how far off it might be. Different kinds of error bars mean different things, so a good chart says which kind it uses.

cards.headline: The cone is a track, not a storm
cards.body: The National Hurricane Center's cone shows where the storm's center will probably go. Its width comes from the forecasters' own track record: it's sized so two-thirds of past forecast errors fall inside. So about one time in three, the center strays outside the cone. It widens further ahead, where past forecasts missed by more.

cards.fact: The storm is bigger than its cone.
cards.context: A hurricane isn't a point. NHC notes that its effects can reach hundreds of miles from the center, well beyond the cone. Sitting just outside the cone doesn't mean you're out of danger. It means the center probably won't pass over you.

cards.headline: Uncertainty: drawn
learned: Error bars show a range, not a size
Charts should say what their bars mean
The cone holds two-thirds of past errors
Storms reach far beyond the cone

questions.prompt: The National Hurricane Center sizes its forecast cone so that what share of past forecast errors fall inside it?

options.label: One-third
options.rationale: That's roughly how often the center strays outside.

options.label: Half
options.rationale: The cone is sized to a bigger share than that.

options.label: All of them
options.rationale: Then the center would never stray outside, but it does.

questions.explanation: The circles are sized so two-thirds of past errors fall inside, so the center strays outside about one time in three.

questions.prompt: Why can a town outside the hurricane cone still be hit hard?

options.label: The cone tracks the center, and the storm's effects reach far beyond it
The cone is drawn too small on purpose
options.rationale: It's sized from past errors; it just shows the center's path.

options.label: Towns outside the cone are never warned
options.rationale: Warnings are separate from the cone.

options.label: Hurricanes always turn at the last moment
options.rationale: That's not why; the cone shows the center, not the storm's size.

questions.explanation: The cone shows the probable path of the storm's center. Effects can reach hundreds of miles from the center, outside the cone.

questions.prompt: Level 9's healthy body temperature was a round 37°C. What would an error bar have added to that number?

options.label: An extra decimal place, like 37.0
options.rationale: More digits suggest precision; a bar shows the range.

options.label: The patients' names
options.rationale: An error bar shows uncertainty, not who was measured.

options.label: Proof that 37°C was exactly right
options.rationale: An error bar shows how far off it might be.

options.label: A range, like 36.5°C to 37.5°C, showing how sharp it was

questions.explanation: A whole-degree 37°C could be anywhere from 36.5°C to 37.5°C. An error bar draws that range instead of hiding it.
